title: Heart Failure & Antiarrhythmics
summary: Drugs that remodel the failing heart and those that control rhythm.

lessons.title: Pathophysiology of Heart Failure

levels.kid:
Heart failure doesn't mean the heart stopped. It means the heart pump is too weak or too stiff to keep up with what the body needs.

When that happens, the body panics a little. It sends out "emergency" chemicals that squeeze blood vessels, speed up the heart and make the kidneys keep water.

That helps for a short time, like shouting at a tired runner. But over months, all that shouting wears the heart out even more. Extra water backs up into the lungs and legs, making it hard to breathe and making ankles puffy.

The best heart failure medicines calm those emergency chemicals down.
levels.hs:
**Heart failure (HF)** is a syndrome where the heart cannot pump enough blood at normal filling pressures. There are two main types based on the **ejection fraction (EF)**, the percent of blood squeezed out with each beat:

- **HFrEF** (reduced EF, 40% or less): the heart muscle is weak, often after a heart attack.
- **HFpEF** (preserved EF, 50% or more): the heart squeezes fine but is stiff and fills poorly. It is common with high blood pressure, obesity, diabetes and older age.

**What goes wrong:** when output falls, the body activates the **sympathetic nervous system**, the **RAAS** and **vasopressin (ADH)**. These raise heart rate, constrict vessels and retain salt and water. At first this keeps blood pressure up. Over time it is harmful: the heart stretches, thickens and scars (**remodeling**), and fluid builds up.

**Symptoms:** shortness of breath, especially lying flat (**orthopnea**) or waking up gasping at night, leg swelling, fatigue, and weight gain from fluid.

The heart fights back by releasing **natriuretic peptides** (BNP) that promote salt loss. Blood BNP levels help diagnose HF.

The key idea for pharmacology: drugs that **block the harmful hormones** (β-blockers, RAAS blockers) help people live longer. Diuretics remove fluid and relieve symptoms but do not lengthen life.
levels.college:
**Definitions.** HFrEF: LVEF 40% or less. HF with mildly reduced EF: 41–49%. HFpEF: 50% or more with evidence of raised filling pressures. Staging runs from A (at risk) to D (advanced). NYHA class I–IV grades symptoms.

**Hemodynamics.** On the Frank-Starling curve, a failing ventricle produces less stroke volume at any preload, and the curve flattens. Higher filling pressures yield congestion with little gain in output. Afterload sensitivity rises, so vasodilation can raise stroke volume in HFrEF.

**Neurohormonal activation:**
- Sympathetic: tachycardia, vasoconstriction, renin release, myocyte toxicity and apoptosis, arrhythmia, β1 receptor down-regulation.
- RAAS: angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction, hypertrophy and fibrosis. Aldosterone retains sodium and promotes myocardial and vascular fibrosis.
- Vasopressin: water retention and hyponatremia, a marker of poor prognosis.
- Endothelin and inflammatory cytokines.
- Counter-regulation: ANP and BNP promote natriuresis and vasodilation. Neprilysin degrades them.

**Remodeling:** eccentric dilation after MI (myocyte slippage, fibrosis), concentric hypertrophy with pressure overload, and a shift from elliptical to spherical geometry that worsens wall stress and functional mitral regurgitation.

**HFpEF** involves impaired relaxation and increased passive stiffness (titin changes, fibrosis), plus vascular stiffness, chronotropic incompetence and systemic comorbidity-driven inflammation. It is heterogeneous, which explains why many neurohormonal drugs that work in HFrEF failed in HFpEF.

**Therapeutic principle:** mortality-reducing drugs in HFrEF block neurohormonal pathways (β-blockers, ACE inhibitors or ARBs or ARNI, MRAs) or work through other mechanisms (SGLT2 inhibitors). Positive inotropes improve hemodynamics acutely but increase mortality with chronic use.

**Precipitants of decompensation:** nonadherence, dietary salt, arrhythmias (especially atrial fibrillation), ischemia, infection, uncontrolled hypertension, and drugs (NSAIDs, thiazolidinediones, non-DHP calcium channel blockers in HFrEF).
levels.phd:
**From pump to neurohormones.** The hemodynamic model treated HF as a pump problem solved by inotropes and vasodilators. Its failure was decisive: chronic milrinone (PROMISE), flosequinan and other inotropes increased mortality, while β-blockers, which acutely depress contractility, reduced mortality and gradually improved EF (reverse remodeling). The neurohormonal model reframed HF as a progressive disorder driven by chronic signaling that injures myocytes.

**β-adrenergic signaling in failure.** Chronic catecholamine exposure up-regulates GRK2, which phosphorylates β1 receptors and recruits β-arrestin, causing desensitization and down-regulation. Persistent β1 signaling through CaMKII promotes apoptosis, hypertrophic gene programs and arrhythmogenic calcium leak. β-blockade restores receptor density and calcium handling over months.

**Calcium cycling and energetics:**
- SERCA2a expression falls and phospholamban inhibition rises, slowing calcium reuptake and impairing relaxation and contractile reserve.
- RyR2 channels become leaky (PKA and CaMKII hyperphosphorylation, loss of calstabin), producing diastolic calcium leak and delayed afterdepolarizations, a substrate for sudden death.
- Enhanced late sodium current loads the cell with sodium, reversing the Na/Ca exchanger.
- The failing heart shifts away from fatty acid oxidation, lowers phosphocreatine-to-ATP ratios and becomes "an engine out of fuel."

**Fibrosis is a drug target.** Aldosterone drives fibroblast activation through mineralocorticoid receptors largely independently of blood pressure. That helps explain MRA benefit at doses with little hemodynamic effect.

**HFpEF phenotypes.** A leading hypothesis (Paulus and Tschöpe) proposes that comorbidity-driven systemic inflammation causes coronary microvascular endothelial dysfunction, reducing NO-cGMP-PKG signaling to myocytes. That leads to titin hypophosphorylation, increased passive stiffness and hypertrophy. Obesity-related, hypertensive, amyloid and other phenotypes behave differently, so a single drug for all HFpEF was unlikely. SGLT2 inhibitors were the first class to benefit HFpEF broadly in trials.
levels.expert:
**Diagnosing the syndrome and its cause.** Echocardiography defines EF, valves and filling pressures. Natriuretic peptides support the diagnosis but have pitfalls: obesity lowers BNP, kidney disease and age raise it, and sacubitril-valsartan raises BNP (a neprilysin substrate) but not NT-proBNP. Always seek the cause: ischemic disease, hypertension, valve disease, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy (anthracyclines, trastuzumab), myocarditis, peripartum cardiomyopathy, and infiltrative disease such as transthyretin amyloid, which has its own therapy.

**Find the trigger of each decompensation:** missed medicines, salt load, new atrial fibrillation, ischemia, infection, thyroid disease, and drugs. NSAIDs, thiazolidinediones, non-DHP calcium channel blockers, class IC antiarrhythmics and some chemotherapy agents worsen HF. A medication reconciliation often explains the admission.

**Neurosurgical connections:**
- **Neurogenic stunned myocardium.** After aneurysmal SAH or other acute brain injury, a catecholamine surge can cause reversible LV dysfunction, troponin release, ECG changes and pulmonary edema, often in a takotsubo-like pattern. It usually recovers over days to weeks. Recognizing it matters because hypotension and pulmonary edema compromise cerebral perfusion during the delayed ischemia window, and inotropes or careful fluid strategy may be needed.
- **Neurogenic pulmonary edema** can occur without significant cardiac dysfunction, through sympathetic surges affecting pulmonary vessels.
- **Anesthesia in HFrEF** carries a high risk of hypotension at induction, and positioning (prone or sitting) shifts preload. Continuing mortality drugs while managing perioperative hemodynamics carefully is the standard.

**Prognostic markers** include hyponatremia, rising natriuretic peptides, worsening renal function, recurrent admissions and an inability to tolerate guideline therapy because of hypotension. These signal advanced HF and the need for specialist evaluation for devices, mechanical support or transplantation.

keyPoints: HFrEF (EF ≤40%), mildly reduced (41–49%), HFpEF (≥50%)
Sympathetic, RAAS and vasopressin activation is compensatory short-term but drives remodeling and death long-term
Natriuretic peptides (BNP) are the counter-regulatory system and a diagnostic marker
Mortality drugs block neurohormones; diuretics relieve congestion only; chronic inotropes increase mortality
Decompensation triggers: nonadherence, salt, AF, ischemia, infection, NSAIDs, TZDs, non-DHP CCBs
Neurogenic stunned myocardium: reversible LV dysfunction after SAH

Admission for HF two weeks after starting high-intensity NSAIDs for back pain
Pulmonary edema and troponin rise on day 2 after SAH
examples.tr: Neurogenic stunned myocardium from a catecholamine surge

lessons.title: Guideline-Directed Heart Failure Therapy

levels.kid:
Doctors have found four kinds of medicine that help people with weak hearts live longer. They call them the four pillars, like four legs holding up a table.

One calms the heart's racing. One blocks the squeezing messenger. One blocks a salty hormone that scars the heart. And one, first made for diabetes, helps the kidneys get rid of sugar and salt and somehow protects the heart too.

Water pills help people breathe easier by peeing out extra fluid, but they are helpers, not pillars.

Using all four together works way better than just one.
levels.hs:
For **HFrEF**, four drug classes each lower the risk of death and hospital stays. Together they are called the **four pillars** of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT):

1. **ARNI** (sacubitril-valsartan), or an ACE inhibitor or ARB if an ARNI isn't possible. Sacubitril blocks neprilysin, the enzyme that breaks down helpful natriuretic peptides.
2. **β-blockers** proven in HF: carvedilol, metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol. They protect the heart from too much adrenaline and gradually strengthen it.
3. **Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs)**: spironolactone or eplerenone. They block aldosterone, reducing scarring and salt retention.
4. **SGLT2 inhibitors**: dapagliflozin or empagliflozin. Originally diabetes drugs, they help HF patients with or without diabetes.

**Loop diuretics** like furosemide relieve fluid overload and breathlessness but don't lengthen life.

Doctors start each drug at a low dose and increase it step by step, checking blood pressure, heart rate, kidney function and potassium. Main side effects: low blood pressure, slow heart rate (β-blockers), high potassium (ARNI and MRA), and genital yeast infections (SGLT2 inhibitors).

For HFpEF, SGLT2 inhibitors are the main proven drug, along with diuretics and treating blood pressure, obesity and atrial fibrillation.
levels.college:
**HFrEF foundational therapy** (each class reduces mortality and hospitalization on top of the others):
- **ARNI.** Sacubitril (prodrug of a neprilysin inhibitor) plus valsartan. In PARADIGM-HF it beat enalapril on cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization. Switching from an ACE inhibitor requires a 36-hour washout because combined neprilysin and ACE inhibition causes angioedema. Risks: hypotension, hyperkalemia, renal function changes.
- **β-blockers.** Carvedilol (nonselective β plus α1 blockade), metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol (β1-selective) reduced mortality (COPERNICUS, MERIT-HF, CIBIS-II). Not all β-blockers work: immediate-release metoprolol tartrate and bucindolol lack equivalent evidence. Start when the patient is euvolemic and stable, and titrate slowly. Expect transient fatigue or fluid retention. EF improves over months.
- **MRAs.** Spironolactone (RALES) and eplerenone (EMPHASIS-HF). Hyperkalemia and worsening renal function require monitoring. Spironolactone's antiandrogenic effects (gynecomastia) are avoided with the more selective eplerenone.
- **SGLT2 inhibitors.** Dapagliflozin (DAPA-HF) and empagliflozin (EMPEROR-Reduced) benefit patients with or without diabetes. Effects: an early, expected eGFR dip; genital mycotic infections; volume depletion; and rare euglycemic ketoacidosis.

**Additional options:** hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate (A-HeFT in Black patients, or when RAAS blockade is impossible), ivabradine (sinus rhythm with persistent high rate despite β-blockade), vericiguat (sGC stimulator after worsening events), and digoxin for symptoms.

**Devices:** an ICD for persistent LVEF 35% or less despite optimized therapy, and cardiac resynchronization for wide-QRS left bundle branch block.

**HFpEF and mildly reduced EF:** SGLT2 inhibitors reduced HF events (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER). The nonsteroidal MRA finerenone reduced worsening HF events (FINEARTS-HF). GLP-1 receptor agonists improve symptoms in obesity-related HFpEF. Diuretics and comorbidity management complete therapy.

**Implementation:** early initiation of all four classes, often within weeks, outperforms slow sequential titration to target before starting the next.
levels.phd:
**SGLT2 inhibitors: benefit without a settled mechanism.** Benefit appears within weeks, independent of glycemia, and is similar in patients without diabetes. Candidate mechanisms include natriuresis and osmotic diuresis targeting interstitial more than intravascular volume; restoration of tubuloglomerular feedback, lowering intraglomerular pressure; a metabolic shift toward ketone and fatty acid oxidation ("thrifty substrate"); reduced epicardial fat and inflammation; increased erythropoietin and hematocrit through relief of renal cortical hypoxia; and a fasting-like state activating SIRT1, AMPK and autophagy. Direct myocardial effects through NHE1 inhibition have been proposed but are debated, because cardiomyocytes express little SGLT2.

**Neprilysin's broad substrate list.** Neprilysin degrades ANP, BNP and CNP, but also bradykinin, substance P, adrenomedullin, glucagon-like peptide-1, angiotensin I and II and endothelin. Inhibiting it alone raises angiotensin II, which is why it must be paired with an ARB. Neprilysin also degrades **amyloid-β**, raising a theoretical concern about Alzheimer pathology. PERSPECTIVE found no difference in cognitive outcomes with sacubitril-valsartan versus valsartan in HFpEF, offering reassurance.

**β-blocker heterogeneity.** Carvedilol adds α1 blockade and antioxidant properties. COMET suggested carvedilol was superior to metoprolol tartrate, though the dose and formulation comparison was contested. Bucindolol in BEST produced marked sympatholysis and no overall survival benefit. Post hoc pharmacogenomics found benefit restricted to carriers of the β1 Arg389 variant, a rare example of genotype-guided response in cardiology. Nebivolol (SENIORS) causes β3-mediated NO release.

**MRAs beyond blood pressure.** RALES used doses with little antihypertensive effect, implicating aldosterone's direct profibrotic action. Finerenone is a nonsteroidal, bulky MRA that binds the receptor differently, recruits different transcriptional cofactors and distributes more evenly between heart and kidney. Preclinical models show stronger antifibrotic effects with comparable or lower hyperkalemia.

**Hyperkalemia as a barrier.** Fear of potassium leads to underdosing of mortality-reducing drugs. Potassium binders were studied for enabling MRA use (DIAMOND), showing that a supportive drug can unlock a life-prolonging one.
levels.expert:
**Getting patients on all four pillars.** The largest gap in HF care is underuse. Clinicians start low doses of multiple classes early, rather than maximizing one before adding the next. STRONG-HF showed that rapid post-discharge up-titration with close follow-up reduced death and readmission. Order is flexible. Many start an SGLT2 inhibitor and β-blocker or MRA quickly, because SGLT2 inhibitors barely lower blood pressure and blunt hyperkalemia.

**Tolerating the expected:**
- A modest creatinine rise after RAAS blockers or SGLT2 inhibitors is hemodynamic and usually acceptable.
- Asymptomatic low blood pressure is not a reason to withdraw therapy. Symptomatic hypotension is, and diuretics may be reduced first if the patient is euvolemic.
- During acute decompensation, β-blockers are usually continued unless there is cardiogenic shock or severe bradycardia. Stopping them increases risk.

**Potassium:** check it early after starting or increasing an MRA or ARNI. Stop supplements, avoid NSAIDs and trimethoprim, and consider a binder before abandoning the MRA.

**SGLT2 inhibitors and surgery.** Euglycemic ketoacidosis can occur when patients are fasting, unwell or undergoing surgery. Ketoacidosis with normal glucose is easily missed. These drugs are held for several days before elective surgery, including neurosurgery, and restarted when eating normally. Check ketones when a perioperative patient is acidotic.

**Neurosurgical notes:** HF patients on GDMT are prone to induction hypotension, especially on ARNI or ACE inhibitor. An MRA plus hypertonic or osmotic therapy for raised ICP can create electrolyte swings. Volume strategy around SAH or tumor surgery needs coordination between the neurocritical care and cardiology teams.

**Reassess after optimization.** Repeat echocardiography after a few months of therapy. Persistent EF of 35% or less prompts ICD and possibly CRT evaluation. An improved EF (HF with improved EF) is not a cure: TRED-HF showed relapse when therapy was withdrawn, so medications continue.

keyPoints: HFrEF four pillars: ARNI (or ACE inhibitor/ARB), evidence-based β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor
Only carvedilol, metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol have β-blocker mortality evidence in HFrEF
ACE inhibitor → ARNI requires a 36-hour washout (angioedema)
MRAs: hyperkalemia; spironolactone gynecomastia, eplerenone more selective
SGLT2 inhibitors help with or without diabetes and in HFpEF; hold before surgery (euglycemic DKA)
Loop diuretics relieve congestion but don't reduce mortality; ICD/CRT after optimization

lessons.title: Digoxin

levels.kid:
Digoxin is one of the oldest heart medicines. It comes from a pretty purple flower called foxglove. More than 200 years ago, a doctor noticed a folk remedy with foxglove helped people with swollen, tired hearts.

Digoxin does two things. It helps the heart squeeze a little stronger, and it slows down a heartbeat that's going too fast.

But the line between helpful and harmful is very thin. Too much can make people throw up, feel confused, see yellow-green colors, and get dangerous heart rhythms.

There's a special antidote that grabs digoxin and pulls it out of action.
levels.hs:
**Digoxin** comes from the foxglove plant (*Digitalis*). William Withering described its use for "dropsy" (fluid buildup from heart failure) in 1785.

**How it works:** digoxin blocks the **sodium-potassium pump (Na/K-ATPase)** in heart cells. Sodium builds up inside, which makes the cell hold onto more **calcium**. More calcium means a **stronger contraction**. Digoxin also boosts the **vagus nerve**, which slows the heart rate and conduction through the AV node.

**Uses:**
- heart failure with reduced EF that still causes symptoms despite the main drugs. It reduces hospital admissions but does not lengthen life.
- slowing the heart rate in atrial fibrillation, especially with heart failure or low blood pressure

**The big problem: a narrow therapeutic index.** The helpful level and the toxic level are close. Toxicity is more likely with:
- kidney problems (digoxin is cleared by the kidneys)
- low potassium, often from diuretics
- older age
- drugs that raise digoxin levels, such as amiodarone and verapamil

**Signs of toxicity:** nausea and vomiting, confusion, blurry vision or seeing **yellow-green** halos, and dangerous rhythms.

**Antidote:** **digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab)**, which bind digoxin in the blood.
levels.college:
**Mechanism.** Digoxin binds the extracellular face of the Na/K-ATPase α subunit, inhibiting the pump. Rising intracellular sodium reduces the driving force for forward-mode Na/Ca exchange, so less calcium leaves the cell. More calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum and released with each beat: **positive inotropy**. Potassium competes with digoxin at the binding site, so **hypokalemia enhances binding and toxicity**.

**Autonomic effects.** Digoxin increases vagal tone and sensitizes baroreceptors, slowing SA node rate and AV nodal conduction and lengthening the AV nodal refractory period. That is why it controls ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation at rest, but less well during exercise when sympathetic drive dominates.

**Pharmacokinetics.** Large volume of distribution (binds skeletal muscle Na/K-ATPase), long half-life that lengthens markedly in renal impairment, mainly renal excretion, and P-glycoprotein transport. Levels are drawn after distribution is complete, several hours after the last dose.

**Interactions that raise levels:** amiodarone, dronedarone, verapamil, quinidine, macrolides, cyclosporine and itraconazole (P-glycoprotein inhibition). Factors that increase toxicity: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, hypothyroidism, renal failure and old age.

**Toxicity:**
- GI: anorexia, nausea, vomiting (often first)
- Neurological: fatigue, confusion, delirium, visual changes (xanthopsia, halos, blurred vision)
- Cardiac: almost any arrhythmia except rapidly conducted supraventricular rhythms. Classic patterns: frequent ventricular ectopy and bigeminy, atrial tachycardia with AV block (increased automaticity plus nodal block), accelerated junctional rhythm, bidirectional ventricular tachycardia and AV block.
- Acute toxicity causes **hyperkalemia** (pumps blocked throughout the body), a marker of severity.

The "scooped" ST segment depression is digoxin **effect**, not toxicity.

**Treatment:** stop digoxin, correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, and give **digoxin immune Fab** for life-threatening arrhythmia, significant hyperkalemia or end-organ dysfunction. After Fab, total digoxin assays become unreliable.

In the DIG trial, digoxin did not change mortality but reduced HF hospitalizations.
levels.phd:
**Isoform pharmacology.** The Na/K-ATPase α subunit has isoforms with distinct tissue distribution: α1 is ubiquitous, α2 predominates in cardiac and skeletal muscle and astrocytes, and α3 is neuronal (also in cardiac conduction tissue in some species). Cardiac glycosides bind the extracellular vestibule in the phosphorylated E2-P conformation, stabilizing it and blocking the cycle. Potassium binding promotes dephosphorylation and lowers glycoside affinity, the molecular basis of the potassium-digoxin antagonism. α2 colocalizes with the Na/Ca exchanger in T-tubule microdomains, so modest α2 inhibition can raise local sodium enough to load calcium without a large global change.

**Neurological relevance of α3.** ATP1A3 mutations cause alternating hemiplegia of childhood and rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism, showing how essential neuronal pump function is. Glycoside neurotoxicity (delirium, visual disturbance, possibly via retinal cone pumps) reflects the drug reaching these isoforms.

**Arrhythmogenesis.** Calcium overload of the sarcoplasmic reticulum produces spontaneous calcium waves that activate inward Na/Ca exchange current, causing **delayed afterdepolarizations** and triggered activity. Bidirectional VT in digoxin toxicity resembles catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, which shares this mechanism, probably reflecting alternating foci in the two fascicles. Enhanced vagal tone simultaneously depresses AV conduction, producing the paradoxical combination of increased automaticity with block.

**Signaling beyond transport.** A fraction of Na/K-ATPase acts as a receptor complex with Src kinase, transactivating EGFR and generating reactive oxygen species at concentrations below those that inhibit transport. Endogenous cardiotonic steroids (an ouabain-like compound, marinobufagenin) have been proposed as natriuretic hormones linked to salt-sensitive hypertension, a controversial idea because of assay difficulties.

**Outcome nuance.** DIG post hoc analyses associated lower serum concentrations with better outcomes and suggested higher mortality in women, possibly from higher achieved levels. Observational data linking digoxin to mortality in atrial fibrillation suffer from confounding by indication. RATE-AF found digoxin comparable to bisoprolol for quality of life in older patients with permanent atrial fibrillation and HF symptoms, with fewer adverse effects.
levels.expert:
**Where digoxin fits now:**
- HFrEF with persistent symptoms despite the four pillars, to reduce hospitalization.
- Rate control in atrial fibrillation when blood pressure limits β-blockers or diltiazem, or as an add-on. It controls resting rate better than exertional rate.
- It is low on the list in younger, active patients, and its benefit depends on keeping levels low.

**Toxicity hides in plain sight.** Classic scenario: an older patient on digoxin and a loop diuretic gets dehydrated, kidney function worsens, potassium drops, and the patient presents with nausea, confusion or visual change. These are easily attributed to infection or dementia. Another common trigger is a newly added interacting drug, especially amiodarone, which is why digoxin is reduced when amiodarone starts. Clinicians consider digoxin whenever an older patient on it has new delirium, GI upset or an unexplained rhythm.

**Acute management:**
- Stop digoxin and check potassium, magnesium, creatinine, a level and an ECG.
- Give Fab for ventricular arrhythmias, high-grade block with instability, significant hyperkalemia in acute toxicity, or end-organ dysfunction. Fab works within minutes to an hour. Renal failure slows clearance of the complex, so rebound can occur.
- Treat hyperkalemia mainly with Fab. Insulin and glucose help. IV calcium was traditionally avoided ("stone heart"), but recent evidence suggests that risk was overstated.
- Avoid electrical cardioversion when possible, because of a risk of ventricular fibrillation in toxicity.
- Chronic toxicity often comes with hypokalemia; replacing potassium carefully is part of therapy.

**Monitoring:** periodic renal function, potassium and levels when clinical status changes. A low target level is used for HF. Levels are interpreted in context: symptoms with a "normal" level can still be toxicity, especially with hypokalemia.

**Neurosurgical angle.** Postoperative patients often have volume shifts, fasting, renal stress and new drugs, all risk factors. Delirium after surgery in an older patient on digoxin warrants a level before attributing it to anesthesia alone.

lessons.title: Vaughan Williams Classes I–IV

levels.kid:
Your heartbeat is run by tiny electrical sparks that travel through the heart in a set order, like a line of dominoes falling.

Sometimes the sparks go wrong: too fast, too messy, or going in circles. That's called an arrhythmia.

Doctors sort rhythm medicines into four main groups, like four teams:
- Team 1 slows the sodium sparks.
- Team 2 blocks adrenaline, the "hurry up" chemical.
- Team 3 makes heart cells rest longer between sparks.
- Team 4 slows the calcium sparks in the heart's relay station.

These medicines can fix bad rhythms, but they can also cause new ones, so doctors are very careful.
levels.hs:
Heart cells fire **action potentials** driven by ions moving through channels. In ventricular muscle, **sodium** rushes in first (phase 0, the upstroke), **calcium** keeps the plateau (phase 2), and **potassium** flows out to reset (phase 3). The SA and AV nodes instead rely on calcium for their upstroke and drift upward on their own between beats (phase 4), which sets the heart rate.

The **Vaughan Williams classification** groups antiarrhythmics by their main action:

- **Class I: sodium channel blockers.** They slow conduction. Subclasses: IA (procainamide, quinidine), IB (lidocaine, mexiletine) and IC (flecainide, propafenone).
- **Class II: β-blockers** (metoprolol, esmolol). They block adrenaline's effects, slowing the SA node and AV node.
- **Class III: potassium channel blockers** (amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide). They lengthen the action potential and the refractory period, so cells can't fire again too soon. They lengthen the **QT interval** on the ECG.
- **Class IV: calcium channel blockers** (verapamil, diltiazem). They slow the AV node.

Some drugs fall outside the scheme, like adenosine, digoxin and magnesium.

**Proarrhythmia** is the big danger: these drugs can cause new arrhythmias. QT-prolonging drugs can trigger a twisting ventricular rhythm called **torsades de pointes**. In the famous **CAST** trial, flecainide-type drugs given after heart attacks increased deaths, even though they suppressed extra beats.
levels.college:
**Class I (sodium channel block)** is subdivided by binding kinetics:
- **IA** (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide): intermediate kinetics, plus potassium channel block that prolongs APD and QT, so torsades is a risk. Quinidine causes cinchonism, diarrhea and thrombocytopenia. Procainamide causes drug-induced lupus and has an active metabolite, NAPA, with class III action. It is useful in pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Disopyramide is strongly anticholinergic and negatively inotropic, exploited in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
- **IB** (lidocaine, mexiletine): fast on and off, shorten APD, selective for depolarized, ischemic tissue and rapid rates. Used for ventricular arrhythmias, little atrial effect. Toxicity is neurological: perioral numbness, tremor, confusion, seizures.
- **IC** (flecainide, propafenone): slow dissociation, marked conduction slowing (QRS widening) even at normal rates, minimal APD change. Contraindicated in structural heart disease and after MI (CAST). In atrial flutter they can slow the flutter rate enough to allow 1:1 AV conduction, so they are given with an AV nodal blocker. Propafenone also has β-blocking activity.

**Class II (β-blockers)** reduce phase 4 slope in nodal cells, slow AV conduction and blunt catecholamine-triggered arrhythmias. They reduce sudden death after MI and in HFrEF and long QT syndrome.

**Class III (potassium channel block, mainly IKr)** prolongs APD and the effective refractory period, terminating re-entry. Drugs: amiodarone (multichannel), dronedarone, sotalol (also β-blocker, renally cleared), dofetilide (renal, started in hospital with QT monitoring), ibutilide (IV for converting AF or flutter). Torsades risk is lowest with amiodarone despite marked QT prolongation.

**Class IV (non-DHP CCBs)** slow AV conduction and terminate AV nodal-dependent re-entry.

**Use dependence and reverse use dependence.** Class I and IV block accumulates at fast rates. Class III drugs prolong APD most at slow rates (reverse use dependence), so torsades typically follows pauses and bradycardia, and efficacy wanes during tachycardia.
levels.phd:
**The limits of Vaughan Williams.** The 1970s scheme assigns each drug one dominant action, but most drugs act on several targets: amiodarone hits classes I through IV, sotalol is II plus III, and propafenone is I plus II. The Sicilian Gambit (1991) proposed a matrix linking drug actions to arrhythmia mechanisms and vulnerable parameters. A 2018 modernized classification (Lei and colleagues) adds class 0 (HCN blockers such as ivabradine), class V (mechanosensitive channel blockers), class VI (gap junction modulators) and class VII (upstream targets such as RAAS blockers and statins), and splits classes by specific channel (for example IKr versus IKur, late versus peak sodium current).

**Guarded-receptor and modulated-receptor hypotheses.** Sodium channel blockers bind preferentially to open and inactivated states, with access via the hydrophilic pathway (through the open pore) or the hydrophobic pathway (through membrane fenestrations). Recovery time constants define subclasses: IB recovers fastest, IC slowest. Depolarized ischemic tissue, with more inactivated channels and slower recovery, is selectively blocked by IB agents. In CAST, IC drugs probably increased mortality by slowing conduction in scarred, ischemic myocardium, creating the substrate for re-entry: a proarrhythmic interaction between drug and disease substrate.

**Mechanism-based torsades.** IKr (hERG, KCNH2) has a large inner cavity with aromatic residues (Y652, F656) that trap many structurally diverse drugs, which is why hERG block is a pervasive liability across medicine. Prolonged repolarization allows L-type calcium channel reactivation, producing early afterdepolarizations. Transmural dispersion of repolarization (midmyocardial M cells prolong most) sustains re-entry. Amiodarone's low torsades rate is attributed to more homogeneous APD prolongation and simultaneous calcium and late sodium current block, lowering dispersion. Risk modifiers include female sex, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, bradycardia, heart failure and subclinical channel variants ("reduced repolarization reserve").

**Regulatory science.** The CiPA initiative replaced reliance on hERG block and QT prolongation alone with in silico models integrating multichannel effects, plus stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte assays. Ranolazine and verapamil block hERG yet carry little torsades risk because concurrent inward current block offsets repolarization delay.
levels.expert:
**Drugs are now second-line for many arrhythmias.** Catheter ablation cures most supraventricular re-entry and is increasingly first-line for atrial fibrillation. Drugs remain essential for acute control, bridging, and patients unsuitable for ablation.

**Choosing rhythm-control drugs for AF by substrate:**
- No structural heart disease: flecainide or propafenone (with an AV nodal blocker), dronedarone or sotalol.
- Coronary disease: avoid class IC. Use sotalol, dofetilide, dronedarone or amiodarone.
- HFrEF: amiodarone or dofetilide. Dronedarone is contraindicated in decompensated or advanced HF.

**QT safety routine:** baseline QTc, potassium and magnesium; review all QT-prolonging co-medications (macrolides, fluoroquinolones, ondansetron, haloperidol, some antidepressants); adjust renally cleared drugs (sotalol, dofetilide); start dofetilide and often sotalol in hospital with telemetry. Torsades is treated with IV magnesium, correction of potassium, removal of the offender, and increasing the heart rate (pacing or isoproterenol) to shorten repolarization. Unstable cases need defibrillation.

**Lidocaine and the neurosurgeon.** Lidocaine and bupivacaine block the same sodium channels in brain and heart. Scalp blocks and large local infiltrations can cause **local anesthetic systemic toxicity**: perioral numbness, tinnitus, agitation, seizures, then bradycardia, conduction block and cardiac arrest. Bupivacaine is especially cardiotoxic because it dissociates slowly. Treatment: stop injecting, secure the airway, control seizures with benzodiazepines, and give **lipid emulsion** early. In cardiac arrest from this cause, resuscitation can be prolonged, and epinephrine is used in reduced doses.

**Wide-complex tachycardia rule:** treat it as VT until proven otherwise. Verapamil given to VT misdiagnosed as SVT with aberrancy can cause collapse. Pre-excited AF (irregular, varying wide QRS) needs procainamide, ibutilide or cardioversion, not AV nodal blockers.

keyPoints: Class I: Na channel blockers (IA quinidine/procainamide/disopyramide; IB lidocaine/mexiletine; IC flecainide/propafenone)
Class II: β-blockers; Class III: K channel blockers (amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide); Class IV: verapamil, diltiazem
IB prefers depolarized, ischemic tissue; IC slows conduction strongly and is contraindicated in structural heart disease (CAST)
Class III prolongs QT; reverse use dependence; torsades after pauses (amiodarone lowest risk)
IC drugs can cause 1:1 conduction of atrial flutter; give with an AV nodal blocker
Torsades: IV magnesium, fix potassium, increase heart rate

lessons.title: Amiodarone, Adenosine and Others

levels.kid:
Two rhythm medicines are famous in hospitals.

Amiodarone is like a Swiss Army knife: it works on lots of different heart channels at once, so it can fix many bad rhythms. But it stays in the body for months and can bother the lungs, thyroid, liver, eyes and skin, so doctors check those often.

Adenosine is the opposite. It lasts only a few seconds! Doctors push it fast into a vein, and it briefly pauses the heart's relay station. That "reset button" can stop certain racing heartbeats. The patient might feel a scary flushing feeling for a moment, then it's gone.
levels.hs:
**Amiodarone** is the most broadly effective antiarrhythmic. It mainly blocks potassium channels (class III) but also blocks sodium channels, β receptors and calcium channels. It treats ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation (including during cardiac arrest) and atrial fibrillation, and it is safer than most antiarrhythmics in patients with heart failure.

The catch is toxicity. Amiodarone contains lots of **iodine**, is stored in fat and stays in the body for months. Side effects:
- **lungs:** scarring (pulmonary fibrosis)
- **thyroid:** either underactive or overactive
- **liver** injury
- **eyes:** corneal deposits, rarely optic nerve damage
- **skin:** sun sensitivity and a blue-gray color
- slow heart rate, and interactions that raise warfarin and digoxin levels

Patients get regular thyroid, liver and lung checks.

**Adenosine** acts on receptors in the **AV node**, briefly blocking conduction. Its effect lasts **seconds**, because cells absorb and break it down quickly. It is pushed rapidly into an IV followed by a saline flush. It stops many **supraventricular tachycardias** that use the AV node as part of their circuit. Side effects are brief: flushing, chest pressure, shortness of breath and a feeling of doom. Caffeine and theophylline block its effect, and it can trigger wheezing in asthma.

**Others:** **magnesium** treats torsades de pointes, **atropine** speeds a slow heart by blocking the vagus nerve, and digoxin slows AV conduction.
levels.college:
**Amiodarone** is a benzofuran derivative with iodine and structural similarity to thyroid hormone. Actions: IKr block (class III) prolongs APD and refractoriness; use-dependent sodium channel block (I); noncompetitive β-adrenergic antagonism (II); L-type calcium block (IV). It also causes vasodilation, which explains IV hypotension (partly from the solvent).

**Pharmacokinetics:** highly lipophilic with an enormous volume of distribution, slow onset with oral therapy (loading required), an active metabolite (desethylamiodarone), and an elimination half-life of weeks to months. It inhibits CYP2C9 (raises warfarin effect), CYP3A4 (raises simvastatin), CYP2D6 and P-glycoprotein (raises digoxin).

**Toxicities and monitoring:**
- pulmonary: interstitial pneumonitis or fibrosis (baseline chest imaging and lung function, investigate new cough or dyspnea)
- thyroid: hypothyroidism (iodine excess, Wolff-Chaikoff) or thyrotoxicosis (type 1 iodine-induced in a diseased gland; type 2 destructive thyroiditis); thyroid tests at baseline and periodically
- liver: transaminase elevation, occasionally hepatitis
- eye: corneal microdeposits (common, usually harmless), optic neuropathy (rare, serious)
- skin: photosensitivity, blue-gray discoloration
- neurological: tremor, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy
- cardiac: bradycardia, AV block; QT prolongation with low torsades risk

**Dronedarone** lacks iodine and is less lipophilic, with fewer organ toxicities but less efficacy. It increased mortality in severe HF (ANDROMEDA) and in permanent AF (PALLAS).

**Adenosine** activates A1 receptors (Gi) in SA and AV nodes, opening acetylcholine/adenosine-activated potassium channels (GIRK) and lowering cAMP and calcium current. The result is transient AV block. Half-life is seconds (cellular uptake and adenosine deaminase). It terminates AV nodal-dependent re-entry (AVNRT, orthodromic AVRT) and unmasks atrial flutter by transiently blocking conduction. Methylxanthines antagonize it; dipyridamole (uptake inhibitor) and carbamazepine potentiate it; transplanted hearts are hypersensitive. Avoid in pre-excited AF and use caution in reactive airway disease.

**Others:** magnesium (torsades, digoxin-induced arrhythmias), atropine (vagal bradycardia, AV nodal block), isoproterenol (bradycardia-dependent torsades), and ivabradine (If block).
levels.phd:
**Amiodarone as a cationic amphiphilic drug.** Its lipophilic benzofuran core and protonatable amine make it a cationic amphiphile that accumulates in lysosomes and inhibits phospholipases, producing **phospholipidosis**. Foamy macrophages and lamellar inclusions in lung, liver and cornea link the drug's chemistry to its organ toxicities. Direct cytotoxicity, oxidative stress and immunological mechanisms add to the picture. Toxicity correlates with cumulative exposure, so lower maintenance intensity reduces risk.

**Thyroid pharmacology.** About a third of the molecule's weight is iodine, and deiodination releases a large iodine load. The drug and its metabolite inhibit type 1 and type 2 5'-deiodinase (reducing T4-to-T3 conversion, raising reverse T3), act as thyroid hormone receptor antagonists, and are directly toxic to thyrocytes. Type 1 thyrotoxicosis (excess synthesis in nodular or autoimmune glands, iodine-induced Jod-Basedow) responds to thionamides. Type 2 (destructive thyroiditis in a normal gland) responds to glucocorticoids. Color-flow Doppler and radioiodine uptake (low in both, because of the iodine load) help distinguish them.

**The dronedarone design lesson.** Removing iodine and adding a methanesulfonyl group reduced lipophilicity and tissue accumulation and eliminated thyroid effects. Efficacy fell and unexpected harms emerged in HF and permanent AF. Chemists attempted to separate amiodarone's benefits from its toxicities, but the two may be intertwined.

**Adenosine signaling.** A1 receptor activation releases Gβγ, which opens GIRK (IK,Ado/ACh) channels in atrial and nodal cells, hyperpolarizing them and shortening atrial APD. Shortening refractoriness can transiently induce AF. Gαi lowers cAMP, opposing catecholamine-stimulated calcium current and If. That is the basis for **adenosine-sensitive VT** from the outflow tracts, a cAMP-mediated triggered activity terminated by adenosine, verapamil or vagal maneuvers. A2A receptors mediate coronary vasodilation (regadenoson, an A2A-selective agonist, is used in stress imaging). A2B and A3 receptors on mast cells and airways explain bronchospasm. Caffeine's arousal effects arise from blocking central A1 and A2A receptors, linking cardiac pharmacology to sleep neuroscience.
levels.expert:
**Amiodarone in practice:**
- Cardiac arrest: given for shock-refractory VF or pulseless VT. Lidocaine is an alternative.
- Stable VT or AF with HFrEF: often the drug of choice because of low proarrhythmia and negative inotropy.
- Long-term therapy: use the lowest effective intensity, with baseline and periodic thyroid and liver tests, chest imaging and lung function when symptoms arise, an eye exam if vision changes, and sun protection. Reduce warfarin and digoxin when starting and check interacting statins. Toxicity can appear or persist months after stopping, so lung or thyroid symptoms in someone who took amiodarone last year still count.
- IV loading can cause hypotension and bradycardia, and phlebitis through peripheral lines.

**Adenosine technique:** large, proximal IV, rapid push followed immediately by a saline flush, with ECG recording, because the transient block can be diagnostic (flutter waves revealed). Warn the patient about a brief, intensely unpleasant sensation. Lower doses are used through central lines, in heart transplant recipients and with dipyridamole or carbamazepine. Higher doses may be needed with heavy caffeine or theophylline. Never give it for irregular wide-complex tachycardia that could be pre-excited AF. Have a defibrillator ready.

**A neurosurgical use.** In clipping complex or giant intracranial aneurysms, or in some arteriovenous malformation work, anesthesiologists can give adenosine to produce brief, controlled cardiac standstill and profound hypotension. This **adenosine-induced flow arrest** softens the aneurysm sac or controls bleeding while the surgeon places a clip, without temporary occlusion or deep hypothermic circulatory arrest. It needs pacing pads, coordination and an understanding of the patient's coronary and conduction status.

**Atropine and bradycardia after brain injury:** bradycardia from vagal stimulation during surgery or raised ICP responds variably to atropine. Persistent bradycardia with hypertension signals the Cushing reflex, a problem of pressure inside the skull, not a drug deficiency.

keyPoints: Amiodarone: class III plus I, II, IV actions; iodine-rich, lipophilic, half-life of weeks to months
Toxicity: lung fibrosis, hypo/hyperthyroidism, liver, corneal deposits, optic neuropathy, blue-gray skin, neuropathy
Amiodarone raises warfarin (CYP2C9) and digoxin (P-gp) levels
Dronedarone: no iodine, less effective; harmful in severe HF and permanent AF
Adenosine: A1 → GIRK in AV node, seconds-long AV block; terminates AVNRT/AVRT; blocked by caffeine/theophylline, potentiated by dipyridamole
Adenosine-induced flow arrest aids complex aneurysm clipping
